title: Vaisheshika (atoms)
hook: a school that wants to list everything there is opens its book with one word you wouldn't expect: dharma

segments.voice: Yesterday Nyaya ended at dusk: the post or the person, and doubt as the doorway to a search that ends in release. A second school opens today.
screen: `NYAYA: FROM DOUBT TO RELEASE.` · `A NEW SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: A sack of rice has split on the kitchen floor. Grains under the stove, in the corners, between the tiles. You crouch and start picking them up, one by one, and a strange thought arrives: this whole sack, this whole meal, is only ever grains. There's a story people tell about the sage who founded today's school: his name, Kanada, came from living on grains, gleaned one by one from harvested fields. Whether or not that's history, it fits. His school would go on to say the world itself is made of tiny grains.
screen: `RICE ON THE KITCHEN FLOOR.` → `ONLY EVER GRAINS.` → `KANADA, THE GRAIN-GATHERER.`

segments.voice: The school is Vaisheshika, and its root text is the Vaisheshika Sutra, credited to Kanada. You might expect it to open with matter. It doesn't. Its first sutra says, in effect: now, therefore, we will explain dharma. The next says what dharma is: that from which come both rising up in this world and the highest good. So before a single atom appears, the school says why it's counting at all. Knowing what the world is made of, and how things really differ, is meant to serve a good life and, finally, freedom. That's the note Nyaya struck, and the two are close neighbors. Later thinkers joined them, so you'll often hear Nyaya-Vaisheshika: one asking how we know, the other asking what there is to know. Then the name. Tradition links Vaisheshika to vishesha, particularity: what makes one thing this one and not that one. Later teachers of the school took it all the way down: two of the tiniest particles of earth, alike in every quality, still aren't copies, and vishesha keeps each one itself. The atoms come tomorrow. But notice the starting point. Not that everything is one blur, but that everything is particular. Carried out of the classroom, that turns tender. The grain on the floor, the stranger on the bus, the person who annoys you: each is really itself, not interchangeable. A school of atoms that begins with dharma refuses to let anything be just another one.
screen: `THE SUTRA OF KANADA.` · `IT OPENS WITH DHARMA.` · `A NEIGHBOR TO NYAYA.` · `VISHESHA: EACH THING IS ITSELF.` · then, large: `NOTHING IS JUST ANOTHER ONE.`

segments.voice: Pick something small near you, a grain of rice, a button, a leaf, and look at it as if it were the only one: its exact edge, its color in this light, the tiny mark no other has. Then, if you like, let one person come to mind and see them the same way, not a type, but this one. If you pray, you can give thanks for this one thing, exactly as it is.
Vaisheshika. The school of Kanada, linked by tradition to vishesha, particularity, and known for its atoms. Its sutra opens with dharma.
Your line: Vaisheshika, atoms. In this school, nothing is just another one. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Vaisheshika is studied in traditional Sanskrit schools alongside Nyaya, often as one joined system, through the Vaisheshika Sutra and its commentaries.

chat.says: A school about atoms starts by talking about dharma? Why?
options: Its first sutra says the counting serves dharma: a good life and, finally, freedom.
Because Kanada thought atoms were gods, so studying them was a kind of worship.
Because its atoms are only a metaphor, and the book is really about manners.

Kanada.meaning: the sage credited with the Vaisheshika Sutra

Vaisheshika.meaning: the school known for atoms and particulars

vishesha.meaning: particularity: what makes this one, not that one

dharma.meaning: right conduct; here, what brings rising and the highest good
